units.title: The menstrual cycle
units.goal: Describe the main cycle events without treating a model as a personal prediction.
text: The menstrual cycle includes changes in the ovaries and uterus. Menstruation is shedding of the uterine lining with bleeding. Day 1 is the first day of a period.

The lining later builds up, and ovulation is release of an egg from an ovary. If pregnancy does not occur, the lining can shed again and a new cycle begins. Detailed hormonal control is outside this introductory lesson.

A 28-day diagram is a teaching example, not a rule for every person. Cycle lengths, bleeding patterns and ovulation timing vary, especially during adolescence. The model must not be used to predict safe days or diagnose a condition.

Periods are a normal biological process, not a reason for shame, exclusion or teasing. Learn the vocabulary respectfully. This app does not collect dates, symptoms or any learner's personal menstrual history.
units.challenge: Explain why a 28-day diagram cannot reliably predict an individual person's ovulation date.

units.title: Care, support & privacy
units.goal: Recognise when support is appropriate without diagnosing symptoms.
text: Cycle variation can occur, particularly in adolescence, but troublesome symptoms deserve support. Pain that disrupts daily activities, concerning heavy bleeding, bleeding between periods or worrying changes should be discussed with a qualified health professional.

A practical school support plan can include access to appropriate menstrual products, clean water, handwashing, private facilities and a trusted adult. Follow product instructions and local health guidance; this lesson does not prescribe medicine.

Do not dismiss severe pain or make a diagnosis from a class discussion. Feeling faint or seriously unwell, or severe bleeding or pain, needs prompt medical attention through a trusted adult or local health service.
Health information is private. A peer can offer respectful support without demanding details, posting photographs, sharing someone else's cycle information or giving unqualified treatment advice.
units.challenge: Write a general school support plan that includes dignity and access to help without recording anyone's private symptoms.

units.title: Fertilisation
units.goal: Describe fusion of sperm and egg at an introductory, non-graphic level.
text: Sperm and eggs are reproductive cells, also called gametes. Fertilisation occurs when a sperm and egg fuse to form a fertilised egg, called a zygote.
In human reproduction, fertilisation usually occurs in an oviduct, also called a fallopian tube. It is not the same process as implantation in the uterus.
The fertilised egg can develop while travelling towards the uterus. This introductory lesson does not describe the detailed stages of early cell division or hormonal control.
The animation is a non-graphic schematic using labelled markers. Its movement and timing are exaggerated, and it is not a guide to predicting pregnancy or assessing an individual.
units.challenge: Explain the difference between ovulation and fertilisation using the correct cell and organ names.

units.title: Implantation
units.goal: Distinguish attachment in the uterus from fertilisation and menstruation.
text: Implantation is attachment and embedding of an early developing embryo, at the blastocyst stage, in the uterine lining. The uterus provides the site; the usual fertilisation site is earlier in the oviduct.

The introductory sequence is ovulation, possible fertilisation, development and travel, then possible implantation. Not every released egg is fertilised, and not every fertilised egg successfully implants.
The lining has a role in supporting early pregnancy. A menstrual-cycle model showing a lining is not itself evidence that implantation or pregnancy has occurred.

The animated marker attaching to the model lining is a simplified illustration, not a medical scan. The lesson omits detailed blastocyst formation and cannot diagnose pregnancy or explain an individual's symptoms.
units.challenge: Put the model's events in order and explain why a diagram cannot confirm that any event occurred in a real person.

units.title: STI knowledge without stigma
units.goal: Recognise uncertainty, prevention principles and appropriate support.
text: Sexually transmitted infections include HIV, gonorrhoea, syphilis and genital herpes. Many infections can have no noticeable symptoms, and symptoms such as unusual discharge, pain when urinating or sores can have more than one cause. Symptoms alone cannot identify or rule out an STI.

HIV and AIDS are not interchangeable terms: HIV infection can lead to AIDS without appropriate management. Effective professional care matters. HIV is not spread by ordinary casual contact such as hugging, so exclusion and stigma are not justified.

Avoiding sexual contact prevents sexual exposure. Correct and consistent condom use reduces the risk of many STIs but does not eliminate every risk, particularly where uncovered skin is involved. Appropriate health services can advise on testing, treatment and available vaccination.

Do not share needles or handle blood and sharps; seek help from trained adults for an exposure concern. Some infections can also be transmitted during pregnancy or birth or through unsafe blood exposure. Do not diagnose peers, share medicines or assume appearance shows infection status.

A personal concern, coercion or harm should be taken to a trusted adult and suitable health or safeguarding service. This is general education, not individual medical advice. The app asks no questions about personal sexual behaviour or symptoms.
units.challenge: Explain why 'looks healthy' cannot establish STI status, and name a respectful route to qualified help.
